The Only Thing I Have To Say About Gamer Gate

The best way to deal with this "Gamergate" crap is the best way to deal with any troll. If you don't know what that is, then chances are you don't know what this entire manufactured controversy is either. For you, I'll summarize, even though you probably don't know what Whoaverse is and you therefore are not reading this.

Ignore trolls. This "controversy" is just a case of media being sleazeballs by giving a voice to sleazeballs, sometimes through those affected by them and sometimes directly. Ignore it and it will all go away, like the boogeyman and Jehova's witnesses.

Don't change anything. Don't avoid anybody. Don't do anything except build up ignore lists. Griefers can only play a grander scale metagame if we enable them.

Great response, I felt more or less the same, but it seems like there are real people out there who are very easily hurt by trolls and unable to filter/ignore them.

As you said, giving any attention to trolls just makes things worse, but this person had people show up at her door. This is no longer trolling and things can get rather ugly if you are a female and maybe living alone.

I think it is on us, guys, and that we need to show our support to female gamers by some sort of viral video campaign. If we are silent and do nothing, things will look much worse then they really are.

That's a good point about people showing up to her door, but publicizing that fact only shows others that by simply knocking on her door and uttering the right words, they'll get attention. Surely she knows people, and those people know others, and so on. It's not necessary that any or every person who might do that obtain her address by questionable means. It's not necessarily true that anybody whom does that is breaking the law.

Wouldn't it make more sense to deny them that attention, while using already-existent services to deal with harassment? "I don't know you. Don't knock on my door again." When they do, call the police. If somebody makes a threat, make a police report.

I'm not trying to be biased with this, but the people involved probably want some of the publicity, to an extant. I'm not saying they want the death threats and all the insults, but the more people that know about your cause, the easier it is to spread the word about it. If Quinn did fuck all those guys to get her game published and good reviews, then she's a shitty person, but she's much more successful because of Gamersgame than she was before all this stuff came to light. Anita Sarkeesian is another example of this. Her Tropes vs Women videos have gotten much more attention than they would have if people didn't come out against her. She now is a consultant for, I believe, DICE and a few other developers about how to not be sexist in video games. and is constantly being nominated for awards, and winning, for being innovative. While I disagree with her opinions, I must say, it's impressive how far she has gotten. Felicia Day hasn't done anything wrong though. She worked hard to create the life she has and she shouldn't live in fear of anything happening just because she is a woman. She's done a lot in the gaming community, and seems like one of the best female, gamer role models. You are correct though that if people would just ignore this all it would blow over quickly.

I wouldn't say she's a shitty person for that, if it in fact did happen. Maybe she just likes to fuck, the partners in question are attractive, and since she's involved with game development those are the people she happens to meet. Derp (right?).

But if her game was published because the people making decisions had a roll in the sheets with her, then I'd say the people who made the decision based on that are shitty people. They turned her joy for sex into something closer to prostitution in that case, and then leaked gossip about it.

But again, that's if it happened at all in the first place. I have doubts that it did.

That entire aspect of the debacle sounds like exactly the kind of made up baloney that sexist people whom also lack intellect and creativity would come up with to slander or libel a successful woman. It also sounds like the exact kind of thing that a woman looking to leverage victimhood feminism for publicity would make up and spread about herself just to say, "See? It does happen! Look what a victim I am!"

When was the last time you heard of anybody caring who a successful woman sleeps with? Marilyn Monroe? That just doesn't happen anymore. It's an antiquated, outmoded tactic that might make an appearance in high school drama but doesn't in the world of grown ups. I don't believe that even happened, but I do believe that somebody spread that rumor to benefit her.

It's just all too cliche and trite. It comes across as theater. I also wouldn't be surprised if the majority of the threats and harassment are originating with the same people writing articles. It looks to me like they can't find a story to fit their narrative, so they created one. That makes more sense than the notion that a bunch of strangers decided to all act in unison against this one person for no reason, to no gain, despite having no motive to even care who she is. This is all noise and no signal.

I agree that if she just enjoys sex and did sleep with all those people then That's not too bad. She would have cheated on her boyfriend, which is super shitty in my opinion, but that's different than professional ethics. Basically, everything you said is right. I wouldn't be surprised if Quinn fabricated some of the initial outrage and blew it out of proportions, but I don't know all the facts about the whole thing.

I hope that this comment doesn't overkill the topic, but there are a few more words I'd like to put here in hope that some people who need them will read them. You and I are on the same page, so I'm not sure if that describes you. But these are things somebody should be saying with all the loudness that the "controversy" engine has.

None of us have all the facts. But I do know that a stranger's sex life is ultimately none of my business, a game that is neither fun nor innovative will not sell, that I see more comments in social media warning of incoming misogynists than any actual misogynists (especially on those pages), and that articles keep being published on this topic because their headlines keep being clicked.

I like that game development and production companies have taken the opportunity to speak out against discrimination. A good thing can't be a bad thing. But there's one other thing too...

Since 1983 when toddler me sat on my dad's lap to play Pacman, I have loved games. I grew up with them and they've been interwoven with my play and work my entire life. Gamers are by far the least bigoted of any pastime I've ever seen. In the clubs, at festivals, at sports arenas and stadiums, in outdoors activities, hobnob high society functions, in casinos, and everywhere else I've seen more bigotry of all kinds. In multiplayer gaming, with few exceptions if somebody says something out of line then another person corrects them or the target of their insult beats them mercilessly in competition.

And that's what gaming has that nothing in the real world can -- the capacity for the victims of bigotry to stomp their tormenters into the ground without causing them any actual harm.

That's how I know this is all baloney. That's how I know that the people who keep it going are doing it for clicks or because they don't actually know gamers.
Sounds like you hit the nail on the head there.
